history.caption: A gate's false-positive rate is set by how many times you look, not by the threshold you set.
history.title: One open gate among many closed

style_when: scale is the story — a port, a refinery, a data centre hall, a rail yard, a skyline of cranes — and the reader needs to feel how big it is
prompt: 200mm telephoto compression in a data hall: a row of identical brushed-steel inspection gates recede along a concrete floor, one gate on the right third propped ajar by a yellow stop-wedge, the other gates closed. Hard directional worklight from the left rakes across the metal, graphite and safety yellow against bone white walls, deep contact shadows, asymmetric off-centre framing, fine film grain, no text, no logos, no people.
negative_prompt: garbled text, random lettering, watermarks, numbers, logos, UI elements
rationale: Compressed telephoto of repeated identical gates conveys the scale of many looks and the one false opening, without resorting to software UI or plumbing.
subject: an industrial inspection gate in a data hall, one of a row, propped ajar by a yellow stop-wedge
core_thesis: A gate's false-positive rate is set by how many times you look, not by the threshold you set, so early stopping requires an interval valid at every look or a fixed horizon.
core_conflict: The tension between continuous monitoring's temptation to stop on success and the fixed-sample statistical guarantee that only holds for one look.
composition: asymmetric off-centre framing with telephoto compression, one open gate on right third, closed gates receding left
alt_text: Your 5% Gate Breaks At 26.1%. A row of industrial inspection gates in a data hall, one propped ajar by a yellow stop-wedge.
caption: Your 5% Gate Breaks At 26.1%: Reading after every case turns a 5% gate into a 26.1% false-positive rate.
title: Your 5% Gate Breaks At 26.1%

review.depicts: A long row of grey metal server-rack doors recedes in telephoto compression along a polished concrete aisle, while the nearest door on the right third of the frame stands propped open against a yellow wedge-shaped stop on the floor.
review.reason: The image literalises the article's own object — a gate — in a compute/data-hall setting and shows it propped ajar and failing to hold, which matches the headline's claim that the 5% gate breaks; the pun is legible to a reader who arrives via the word 'gate' in the headline, though the statistical mechanism itself (repeated looks, 26.1%) is not depictable and is carried only by the metaphor.
